what: Budget 2026 live updates: Chalmers on media blitz to sell ‘contentious’ budget; shadow treasurer says Coalition will try to block tax reforms

clean_source_blocks.text: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has indicated the government will build on its Working Australians Tax Offset (WATO) in future budgets, allowing it to offset bracket creep. Follow our live blog for the latest reactions and updates from the aftermath of the budget announcement. Choose what information you see below by using filters Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says the government's changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax won't help younger Australians get into the housing market. "According to the government's own budget documents, 35,000 fewer homes will be built as a consequence of these tax changes," he told ABC Radio National Breakfast. "The treasurer has been at pains to say that supply is the big problem we have with housing." Wilson also says that new tax changes will drive rents up and that young Australians will be "kneecapped on multiple fronts".

"As they're saving for a deposit, they're going to pay higher rents. Then the government is going to apply more taxes on their first home deposit if it's invested, and they're going to then go on and build fewer homes, which means that it's going to be less likely young Australians will be able to buy one." Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the government isn't changing tax arrangements to family homes and inheritance. The government backflipped on an election promise not to make changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax in last night's budget. Asked on Sky News whether there are any other taxes in the government's sights, Chalmers says the government isn't seeking changes to the settings of home and inheritance tax.

"We're not changing the arrangements when it comes to the family home. We're not changing arrangements when it comes to things like inheritances, all of those sorts of things that people push around on social media," Chalmers says. Anthony Albanese was asked earlier on News Breakfast why now was the time to make changes to property taxes. He said the government had thrown everything at the housing market, but it still wasn't enough to get young people onto the property ladder. "What this change will do is allow 75,000 young Australians to buy their own home. The Australian dream of owning your own home is something that was increasingly disappearing, and importantly, that creates social dislocation," he said.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has indicated the government will build on its Working Australians Tax Offset (WATO) in future budgets, allowing it to offset bracket creep.

Follow our live blog for the latest reactions and updates from the aftermath of the budget announcement.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says the government's changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax won't help younger Australians get into the housing market.

"According to the government's own budget documents, 35,000 fewer homes will be built as a consequence of these tax changes," he told ABC Radio National Breakfast.

"The treasurer has been at pains to say that supply is the big problem we have with housing."

Wilson also says that new tax changes will drive rents up and that young Australians will be "kneecapped on multiple fronts".

"As they're saving for a deposit, they're going to pay higher rents. Then the government is going to apply more taxes on their first home deposit if it's invested, and they're going to then go on and build fewer homes, which means that it's going to be less likely young Australians will be able to buy one."

Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the government isn't changing tax arrangements to family homes and inheritance.

The government backflipped on an election promise not to make changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax in last night's budget.

Asked on Sky News whether there are any other taxes in the government's sights, Chalmers says the government isn't seeking changes to the settings of home and inheritance tax.

"We're not changing the arrangements when it comes to the family home. We're not changing arrangements when it comes to things like inheritances, all of those sorts of things that people push around on social media," Chalmers says.

Anthony Albanese was asked earlier on News Breakfast why now was the time to make changes to property taxes.

He said the government had thrown everything at the housing market, but it still wasn't enough to get young people onto the property ladder.

"What this change will do is allow 75,000 young Australians to buy their own home. The Australian dream of owning your own home is something that was increasingly disappearing, and importantly, that creates social dislocation," he said.

"If you have two classes of people — home owners and non–home owners — permanently shut out of the housing market, then that doesn't do anything for social cohesion.
